claim: National Assembly has Senate (3 Senators per State, 1 FCT) and House of Representatives (360 members); exercises legislative powers, passes bills, controls Consolidated Revenue Fund, and investigates.
note: Also matches JAMB Syllabus Part 1 Topic 4(a) and Part 2 Topic 6(a).

claim: Federal executive power vests in the President (exercised with Vice-President and Ministers); State executive power vests in the Governor (with Deputy Governor and Commissioners).
note: Also matches JAMB Syllabus Part 1 Topic 4(b) and Part 2 Topic 6(b).

claim: Judicial power vests in superior courts of record (Supreme Court, Court of Appeal, Federal High Court, National Industrial Court, State High Courts) over disputes including government vs persons; ouster clauses barred.
note: Section 6(5)(cc) National Industrial Court inserted by Third Alteration Act 2010.

claim: Separation of personnel: National Assembly or State Assembly members appointed as Federal Ministers or State Commissioners vacate their legislative seats.
note: Prevents dual membership in legislature and executive in Nigeria's presidential system.

claim: Checks and balances: President has 30 days to assent/veto; 2/3 of each House overrides veto; Senate confirms Ministers (s. 147(2)) and senior judges (s. 231); courts void unconstitutional laws (ss. 1(3), 4(8)).
note: Section 147(2) & (7) updated by Fifth Alteration (No. 23) Act 2023; s. 292(1)(a)(i) updated by Third Alteration Act 2010.

claim: Veto override requires passing the bill again by two-thirds majority of each House of the National Assembly; Chief Justice does not assent to bills; referendums apply to s. 8 state/LG creation.
Senate confirms Ministerial nominees (s. 147(2)) and National Assembly investigates appropriated fund spending (s. 88); Governors are elected (s. 178) and President commands Armed Forces (s. 218).
Removal of President/Vice-President: 1/3 notice, 2/3 motion in each House, CJN appoints 7-person panel, 2/3 adoption in each House removes; s. 143(10) bars court review of proceedings.
Separation of powers allows inter-branch constitutional checks while barring dual legislative-ministerial membership.
A National Assembly member appointed Minister is deemed to have resigned their legislative seat upon taking the oath of office.
Constitutional supremacy: the Constitution is supreme and binds all authorities and persons; unconstitutional takeover is barred; any inconsistent law is void to the extent of inconsistency.
note: Also matches JAMB Syllabus Part 1 Topics 8 & 9.

claim: JAMB syllabus classifies constitutions into Written, Unwritten, Rigid and Flexible.
note: Country examples of unwritten/flexible constitutions omitted pending textbook verification.

claim: The 1999 Constitution is a single written codified document organised into a Preamble, Chapters I–VIII, and Seven Schedules.
note: Provides a single text for judicial testing under s. 1(3).

claim: Rigid amendment procedure: general alterations require 2/3 of all members of each House plus 2/3 of State Houses of Assembly; altering s. 8, s. 9, or Chapter IV requires 4/5 of all members of each House plus 2/3 of State Houses; ordinary bills need simple majority of those present.
note: Demonstrates rigidity compared with ordinary legislation.

claim: Altering any Fundamental Right in Chapter IV requires four-fifths majority of all members of each House of the National Assembly and approval by two-thirds of all State Houses of Assembly.
Any State Law inconsistent with the Constitution is void to the extent of the inconsistency under constitutional supremacy.
Under s. 9(4), the two-thirds and four-fifths majorities are calculated out of ALL members specified in ss. 48 and 49 notwithstanding any vacancy.
Classification by form (written vs unwritten) is distinct from amendment difficulty (rigid vs flexible); Nigeria's 1999 Constitution is both written and rigid.
note: Cross-checked with JAMB Government Syllabus Part 1 Topic 8.

claim: Constitutional alteration majorities in s. 9(2)–(3) use total membership specified in ss. 48–49 regardless of vacancies, unlike s. 56(1) simple majorities of members present and voting.

Rule of law foundations: constitutional supremacy (s. 1(1)), ban on ousting court jurisdiction (s. 4(8)), judicial power over government-citizen disputes (s. 6(6)(b)), equality before the law (s. 17(2)(a)), and independent accessible courts (s. 17(2)(e)).
note: Also matches JAMB Syllabus Part 1 Topic 9.

claim: Chapter IV protects life (s. 33), dignity/no torture or forced labour (s. 34), personal liberty (s. 35: silence, written grounds in 24 hrs, court within 1 day if court <= 40 km or 2 days otherwise), and fair hearing (s. 36: presumption of innocence, no retroactive crime).
note: Trial limit if held without bail is 2 months (s. 35(4)(a)); capital offences excluded from s. 35(4) (s. 35(7)(a)).

claim: Chapter IV protects privacy (s. 37), thought/conscience/religion (s. 38), expression/press (s. 39), peaceful assembly/association (s. 40), movement (s. 41), freedom from discrimination (s. 42), and property with prompt compensation (ss. 43–44).
note: Also matches JAMB Syllabus Part 1 Topic 9.

claim: Section 45(1) permits laws reasonably justifiable in a democratic society restricting ss. 37–41 for defence, safety, order, morality, health, or others' rights; s. 46 grants High Court original jurisdiction and legal aid.
note: Also matches JAMB Syllabus Part 1 Topic 9.

claim: Under s. 35(5)(a), where a competent court lies within a 40 km radius of the place of arrest or detention, 'a reasonable time' to bring the suspect before a court is 1 day.
Section 42 (freedom from discrimination) is in Chapter IV and directly enforceable in a High Court under s. 46, whereas Chapter II provisions (ss. 17, 18, 20) are non-justiciable under s. 6(6)(c).
Chapter II Directive Principles (ss. 13–24) are barred from judicial enforcement under s. 6(6)(c), unlike Chapter IV Fundamental Rights (ss. 33–46).
Even during a s. 305 state of emergency, s. 45(2) proviso forbids any derogation from s. 36(8) (no retroactive criminal offences) or from s. 33 except deaths from lawful acts of war.

Section 45(1) allows restricting ss. 37–41 only by a law reasonably justifiable in a democratic society for defence, public safety, public order, public morality, public health, or protecting others' rights.

Citizenship by birth: born in Nigeria before 1 Oct 1960 with indigenous parent/grandparent (and parent/grandparent born in Nigeria); born in Nigeria after 1 Oct 1960 with Nigerian citizen parent/grandparent; or born abroad with Nigerian citizen parent.
note: Also matches JAMB Syllabus Part 1 Topic 11(a).

claim: Citizenship by registration (s. 26) covers foreign women married to Nigerian citizens and full-age persons born abroad with a Nigerian grandparent; naturalisation (s. 27) requires 15 continuous years residence (or 12 months + 15 in 20 years), Governor's local-acceptance attestation, character, contribution, and Oath.
note: Also matches JAMB Syllabus Part 1 Topic 11(a).

claim: Dual citizenship (s. 28) is permitted for birth citizens while non-birth citizens must renounce prior non-birth citizenship within 12 months; renunciation (s. 29); President may deprive naturalised/registered citizens on stated grounds (s. 30), never birth citizens.
note: Also matches JAMB Syllabus Part 1 Topic 11(c).

claim: Citizen duties include obeying the Constitution, respecting national symbols, defending Nigeria, respecting others, assisting law enforcement, and paying tax promptly (s. 24); State's primary purpose is security and welfare of the people (s. 14(2)(b)).
note: Also matches JAMB Syllabus Part 1 Topic 11(b), (d), (e).

claim: A child born in Nigeria after 1 Oct 1960 to two non-Nigerian parents with no Nigerian grandparent is not a citizen by birth under s. 25(1)(b) and must apply under s. 27 if eligible.
Under s. 30(1), the President may deprive a naturalised citizen sentenced to imprisonment for at least 3 years within 7 years of naturalisation; citizens by birth are excluded from deprivation.
Post-1960 birth in Nigeria without a Nigerian citizen parent or grandparent does not confer citizenship by birth.

Non-birth citizens forfeit Nigerian citizenship if they keep or acquire non-birth foreign citizenship beyond 12 months (s. 28), and only birth citizens qualify for President (s. 131(a)) or Governor (s. 177(a)).
Residency requirement for naturalisation is 15 continuous years immediately preceding application, or 12 continuous months plus an aggregate of 15 years in the preceding 20 years.
Universal adult suffrage at age 18: every Nigerian citizen aged 18 residing in Nigeria at registration is entitled to register and vote in federal, state, and local elections.
note: Also matches JAMB Syllabus Part 1 Topic 12(a)–(b).

claim: Minimum candidate ages after 4th Alteration No. 27 (2017): House of Representatives 25, State House of Assembly 25, Senate 35, Governor 35, President 35; all need School Certificate or equivalent and party sponsorship.
note: Also matches JAMB Syllabus Part 1 Topic 12(b).

claim: Presidential winner needs majority/highest votes plus >= 1/4 in at least 2/3 of all 36 States and FCT (s. 134); Governorship winner needs highest votes plus >= 1/4 in at least 2/3 of all LGAs in the State (s. 179); run-off within 21 days otherwise.
note: Also matches JAMB Syllabus Part 1 Topic 12(c).

claim: INEC (Chairman >= 40 yrs, 12 National Commissioners >= 35 yrs, 1 REC per State/FCT >= 35 yrs) runs federal and state elections; SIEC (Chairman + 5–7 members) runs local council elections; petitions filed in 21 days, tribunal 180 days, appeal 60 days; Court of Appeal hears Presidential petitions first.
where: ss. 153, 154, 158, 197, 239, 285; 3rd Sched. Pt. I Item F paras. 14–15, Pt. II Item B paras. 3–4
note: First Alteration 2010 substituted para. 14; Second Alteration 2010 substituted ss. 239 and 285(1)–(7).

claim: Recall of a National Assembly member requires a petition signed by > 1/2 of registered constituency voters, verified by INEC, and approved by simple majority in a referendum within 90 days.
House of Representatives minimum age is 25 years under s. 65(1)(b) as altered by 4th Alteration No. 27 (2017); 18 is voting age, 30 was pre-2017, 35 applies to Senate/Governor/President.
4th Alteration No. 27 reduced age for President (40 to 35), House of Representatives (30 to 25), and State House of Assembly (30 to 25), leaving Senate and Governor at 35.

SIEC conducts Local Government Council elections in each State (3rd Sched. Pt. II Item B para. 4); Court of Appeal has exclusive original jurisdiction over Presidential election petitions (s. 239(1)).
where: ss. 197, 239(1), 285; 3rd Sched. Pt. II Item B para. 4

claim: The Court of Appeal has exclusive original jurisdiction over Presidential and Vice-Presidential election petitions under s. 239(1), with appeal to the Supreme Court under s. 233(2)(e).

Section 40 protects forming political parties, trade unions, and interest associations; s. 221 prohibits any association other than a political party from canvassing for votes or contributing to party/election funds.
note: Also matches JAMB Syllabus Part 1 Topics 13–14.

claim: Parties must register officers and constitution with INEC (alterations within 30 days), open membership to all citizens, avoid ethnic/religious names/logos, locate HQ in Abuja, hold officer elections every <= 4 years, reflect >= 2/3 of States + FCT in executive, and conform aims to Chapter II.
note: Also matches JAMB Syllabus Part 1 Topic 13 and Part 2 Topic 8.

claim: Parties must file financial statements with INEC, transfer foreign funds to INEC within 21 days (s. 225), never form quasi-military groups (s. 227), and face INEC de-registration if breaching rules or failing performance thresholds (s. 225A).
note: Section 225A inserted by Fourth Alteration (No. 9) Act 2017.

claim: Elective candidates must belong to and be sponsored by a political party; legislators who defect before term expiry vacate their seat unless due to a division in the old party or a merger.
note: Also matches JAMB Syllabus Part 1 Topic 13 and Part 2 Topic 8.

claim: While interest associations may form under s. 40 and lobby lawmakers, contributing funds to candidate election expenses violates s. 221.

Political party executive committees must reflect federal character by belonging to at least two-thirds of all States and FCT (s. 223(2)(b)), with Abuja HQ (s. 222(f)) and <= 4-year officer elections (s. 223(2)(a)).
A defecting legislator retains their seat only when joining another party results from a division in the sponsoring party or a merger of parties/factions.
Section 40 proviso preserves INEC's powers over unrecognised parties, and s. 225A empowers INEC to de-register parties failing registration or election thresholds.
Any funds or assets remitted to a political party from outside Nigeria must be paid or transferred to INEC within 21 days of receipt.
Nigeria is one indivisible Sovereign Federation of 36 States, the FCT Abuja, 768 Local Government Areas, and 6 FCT Area Councils (774 local areas total).
where: ss. 2(1)–(2), 3(1), 3(6); First Schedule Parts I & II
note: Also matches JAMB Syllabus Part 2 Topics 9(b) & 11(b).

claim: Exclusive Legislative List (68 items, 2nd Sched. Pt. I) belongs solely to National Assembly (s. 4(2)–(3)); Concurrent List (Pt. II) is shared with federal supremacy on conflict (s. 4(5)); residual unlisted matters belong to State Assemblies (s. 4(7)(a)).
where: s. 4(2)–(7); Second Schedule Parts I & II
note: Also matches JAMB Syllabus Part 2 Topic 9(b).

claim: Federal Character (s. 14(3)–(4)) requires diversity in federal/state bodies; Federation Account (s. 162) shares revenue among Federal, State, and Local Governments with at least 13% natural-resource derivation.
where: ss. 14(3)–(4), 162(1)–(3); 3rd Sched. Pt. I Items C & N
note: Also matches JAMB Syllabus Part 2 Topic 9(d).

claim: Section 7(1) guarantees democratically elected local government councils; Fourth Schedule assigns markets, motor parks, cemeteries, street naming, vital registration, sanitation, and primary education/health participation; funded via Federation Account/State Joint Account and State revenue.
note: Also matches JAMB Syllabus Part 2 Topic 11(b).

claim: Under s. 4(5), when a State Law conflicts with a valid National Assembly law on a Concurrent matter, the Federal law prevails and the State Law is void to the extent of the inconsistency.

Markets, motor parks, and cemeteries sit in Fourth Schedule (LG functions), whereas currency (Item 15), defence (Item 17), aviation (Item 3), diplomatic representation (Item 20), and external affairs (Item 26) sit on the Exclusive Legislative List.
where: Second Schedule Pt. I Items 3, 15, 17, 20, 26; Fourth Schedule para. 1(c), (e)

claim: Creating a new Local Government Area begins in the State House of Assembly under s. 8(3), and requires an Act of the National Assembly under s. 8(5)–(6) to update s. 3 and the First Schedule.
Concurrent powers (2nd Sched. Pt. II) are shared between Federation and States (with s. 4(5) federal prevalence), whereas residual powers (unlisted matters) belong solely to States under s. 4(7)(a).
Proviso to s. 162(2) requires the revenue-allocation formula to constantly reflect derivation at not less than 13 per cent of Federation Account revenue accruing directly from natural resources.
